The kidnapper has taken a family member hostage—not the daughter—and demands that 100 million yen be brought alone; crucially, the demand specifies that the daughter herself must personally deliver the money, alone. The daughter, who is safe and free, begs her father to pay so that the hostage's life will be spared. The father realizes that complying would mean sending his daughter alone into the kidnappers' hands and danger—the very person he most needs to protect would become the lone courier walking into the trap. So he refuses to pay, choosing to keep his daughter out of danger even though this means the family-member hostage's life remains at risk.

The daughter, who is otherwise safe and free, begs her father to pay so the hostage's life is spared. The father refuses because complying would require sending his daughter alone into the kidnappers' hands, placing her in grave danger (and exposing the family). Rather than pay and put his daughter at risk, he decides the ransom should not be paid, accepting that the family-member hostage remains in peril.

The kidnapper holds a family member hostage—someone other than the daughter—and demands that 100 million yen be brought alone, specifying that the daughter herself must deliver it alone. The daughter, who is safe and free, begs her father to pay so that the hostage's life will be spared. The father refuses because the demand, if met, would require sending his daughter alone into the kidnappers' hands: she would be the lone courier walking into danger, where she could be seized or harmed. Rather than pay and expose his daughter to that danger, he decides the ransom should not be paid, even though this leaves the family-member hostage at risk.
